comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Ryan brought the bus back from Soulspeed today reporting another inverter overtemp "limp mode" — an issue we hadn't seen in weeks since switching the reservoir return line from 3/8" to 5/8". I verified the basics first: coolant reservoir full and flowing well, no bubbles, and the coolant fan operating.
A few observations from digging in: the inlet and outlet are swapped on the inverter (probably doesn't matter, but we could set it to Tesla spec), and we run the inverter and motor in series while Tesla actually plumbs them in parallel. Neither seems likely to fix the inverter temp, but both are options to test.
I ran two controlled test drives at 100°F ambient to isolate whether airflow (the skidplate) is the culprit.
Run 1 (skidplate on): inverter started at 109°F and hit the 160°F overtemp limp mode after 13 minutes of hard-ish driving. Motor climbed from 163°F to 232°F — still mid-gauge in the Ampere GUI. Notably, the temperature creep is slow and steady, not "peaky" like Connolly was with its restrictive return line (30°F swings with throttle); Ferdman barely reacts to power input or off-throttle periods.
Run 2 (skidplate removed): inverter started at 104°F, motor at 165°F. Took 17 minutes / 2.5 laps of the same loop to hit limp mode at 160°F inverter, 241°F motor.
Conclusion: removing the skidplate bought roughly 25% more time/distance before limp mode, but didn't prevent it. Airflow is a contributing factor, not the root cause. Next candidates to test: correcting the inverter inlet/outlet to Tesla spec and re-plumbing the motor/inverter from series to parallel.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Claude:
"Fix cooling. Stop chasing signals.
Three reasons, and the third decides the order.
1. The bus has given up what it has. We now know the derate driver (motor temp), the inverter's limit and which sensor it uses (module, 80 °C), and the coolant temperature (RTD1). The remaining signal mysteries — hot-spot reading zero, the duplicated coolant field, AEM's channel labels — wouldn't change a single action. Chasing them further is bookkeeping.

2. The cooling system is already flat out and losing. Pump at 100 % duty and ~6,500 rpm for the entire evening — never modulated, no reserve. Module-to-coolant delta normal at 3.2 °C median. So heat transfer out of the modules is fine and the pump is maxed; the constraint is heat-rejection capacity, not control and not the interface.

3. Order matters — settings first would make it worse. Raising the derate thresholds hands torque back, which puts more heat into a loop that's already out of margin, while the inverter sits at its 80 °C limit. Cooling first isn't just safer, it's the only sequence that isn't self-defeating. And it pays twice: cooler coolant means a cooler motor, which backs the derate off on its own and gives you some torque back without touching a single parameter.

Start here — Fan1 is never commanded
Not once, at any coolant temperature, all the way to 65 °C with 40 °C ambient. Fan2 runs continuously. Either this car only has one fan wired to the Fan2 output, or there's a second fan that isn't being asked to run — which would be free capacity sitting idle. That's a five-minute check and it's the cheapest possible outcome.

After that, in cost order:
Airflow at the radiator— blockage, missing shroud, or hot air recirculating. At 40 °C ambient every degree of approach matters.
Loop topology— is the inverter fed before or after the motor? RTD1 is coolantbefore the inverterand it's already 62 °C. If a 129 °C motor sits upstream, the inverter is being handed pre-heated coolant and can never win. Worth confirming the plumbing order; if it is motor-then-inverter, re-routing or splitting the loop is likely the single biggest lever.
Radiator capacity— to hold modules under 70 °C you need coolant near 50 °C, which is only 10 °C above that day's ambient. That may simply be more than this radiator can do, in which case it's a sizing decision.
Actual flow— the pump is commanded 100 %, but air lock or a restriction would still starve it."
Me:
I'm not sure what is meant by 'modules'. Is claude confusing the motor circuit and the battery circuit? Claude is only looking at the motor circuit, correct?

Not sure what is referred to as 'fan 1' and 'fan 2', but I can confirm that all 3 fans come on as expected. There are currently two motor radiators, the original and the temporary secondary, both come on at the same time.
Airflow at both radiators is questionable. We have one small radiator horizontally under the car, and one in the cubby on the rear driver's side.
Inverter is fed before the motor. Circuit currently:
Pump > inverter > motor > secondary rad > ovar > primary rad > reservoir
Radiator capacity... I don't believe this is significantly different than any of our other cars.
Air lock or starvation. I see no evidence of flow restriction. In the reservoir there are no bubbles, flow looks good, level stays steady.




My thoughts...
Airflow on the primary radiator does appear to have an effect. Removing the skidplate increased the time-to-overheat by 25%.
Adding a secondary radiator did make a significant improvement in the symptoms with no other changes Prior to that change coolant temps were over 160F and the symptom was inverter overtemp errors and the vehicle shutting off. Adding a second radiator in a spot with minimal airflow temps dropped by 20F. Not enough to prevent derating, but better than before.
The differences between this car and our other cars:
SDU
Radiator placement


Things to test:
I can swap the inverter inlets and see if that helps. As I mentioned before, I plumbed it backwards to how Tesla runs it. Could have an effect.

Today:
Swapped the inlet on the inverter.
Removed the cover on the LH fenderwell to increase airflow.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
I did my overheating loop with heavy throttle application. No overheating, but no game-changing improvement on cooling. GUI temps are still roughly where they were prior to the last round of tunes. I did not observe any de-rating, but acceleration is still abnormal so I can't say for sure.

Maximum inverter temp on GUI was 135 (typically hovers around 129F) and maximum motor temp on GUI was 200F in a 15 minute test drive. Ambient temp 98F.

That said, we're really down to the wire for an early September soft delivery. We need the radiator brackets designed immediately so they can be ordered and installed next week.

There is the possibility that the two derales are insufficient even once we get the tuning ironed out, but if we wait for that definitive data we will not be able to meet our soft-delivery deadline.

Whatever we're going to do we need to decide today. I'm of the opinion that we should pull the trigger and have @geoff raynak or @Marshall Carter design the wheel-well radiator mount brackets and get them rush-shipped here so I can take care of it next week. Worst case scenario, we have to figure out a solution for the de-rating down the line, but Ferdman can drive it in the meantime. The inverter-overheat-shutdown has been resolved at least. (edited)

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Walked Andrew through the vehicle requirements sheet and filled in all the information possible. Went to flash inverter firmware, cable wouldn't connect physically, looks like the wrong gender. Made quick cable changer. Connected to inverter, pulled EEPROM backups for the main settings, RTD calibrations, and control loop settings. Flashed firmware 6533 and started on the EEPROM combing. Had Claude look at the EEPROM compare tool since it wasn't working for some reason. Compared the Ampere, Moment, and Stock W EEPROM files and decided on an updated blend with weight towards the Ampere settings, made a Master EEPROM column in the startup sheet to permanently capture these. Flashed and backed up everything. Moved on to the VCU, flashed the latest firmware, transfered settinngs from the vehicle requirements sheet and noted with comments where it was lackinng / not super clear. Transfered clear settings to the VCU and marked ones that needed to be reviewed at a later date. Upgraded the PMU's to the latest firmware and flashed the Preheim calibration, which matches closest. Later this week when Preheim HVAC is finished it should be considered to re-flash that program over to here if zero changes have been made to McDonough. Moved over to OBD port which is not reading the PMU CAN but was able to use the PMU checkout box to monitor current while Andrew forced on all channels controlled by the VCU. Started to hookup HV and ran into an HVIL issue, narrowed it down to an IMD box which checked good earlier. Either it's a different IMD box that was actually installed in the vehicle or the vehicle harness has an issue.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Measured CAN network resistances and found CAN3 at 105 Ohms. Temporarily added a resistor to CAN3 to correct the termination. Found PMU CAN1 was flipped high and low causing the laptop to not connect, had brandon fix that. Verified HVIL now satisfied with Daves fix, plugged in the rest of the HV acessories. Enabled HV from the VCU and watched precharge. Verified L2 charging and DCDC output and marked off in the sheet. Discovered bug where PMU was sending output status 1 for all channels, corrected. Will need to fix on three other vehicles. Monitored VCU while testing brake switch. Ended up overriding from the VCU to move on. Calibrated the resolver and continued testing brakes with Dave. Took the vehicle for a test drive and updated the punch card.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Drew up HVAC summary diagram for understanding of which control needs to be configured where. Corrected incorrect VCU options marked off as done during rush last week. Verified all input switches making it to the right controller and all outputs switching on the correct device. Watched AC cycles with Dave & adjusted setpoints per his suggestion. Tested cabin heat, drawing 2kW and internally shutting off at 70C, might be a blend door problem that is not removing the heat from the heater core.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text:
Removed the temp temperature logger from Preheim and wired up some thermistors to take the place of the permanent ones in the battery box. Adjusted the logger setup slightly and setup to log temps on Hastert out in the sun. Temperature results at 5pm:

Top of Dash: 32.9 C
Top of Battery Box: 36.9 C
Side of Battery Box: 34.6 C
Side of Battery Box (In the air): 41.8 C

Looks like the air around the box is significantly hotter, test might not have ran long enough. Should re-try on the Lotus.
